clinicalPearls: Duplications are spherical (cystic, commoner) or tubular structures that arise on the mesenteric border of the native bowel and share a common muscular wall and blood supply with it.
The ileum is the single most frequent site, but duplications can occur anywhere from the oral cavity to the anus; most are non-communicating with the true lumen.
The epithelial lining is typically alimentary mucosa, and ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue is common, predisposing to peptic ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding.
Ultrasound shows the classic 'gut signature' or double-wall sign — an inner echogenic mucosa with an outer hypoechoic muscular rim — which strongly suggests the diagnosis.
Presentation is usually in infancy or early childhood with a palpable mass, obstruction, or bleeding, but incidental adult diagnosis is well recognised.
Complications include bowel obstruction, volvulus, intussusception (the cyst acting as a lead point), and pain from distension or intracystic haemorrhage.

Thoracic and thoraco-abdominal (oesophageal) duplications are frequently associated with vertebral anomalies and a persistent connection to the spinal canal, in keeping with the split-notochord theory.
A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan can localise ectopic gastric mucosa when bleeding is the presenting feature.
reference.pathophysiology: Intestinal duplications are congenital malformations whose precise embryogenesis is uncertain; leading theories include aberrant recanalisation of the gut lumen, persistence of embryonic diverticula, partial twinning, and the split-notochord hypothesis for the thoracic and thoraco-abdominal forms associated with vertebral defects. The lesion invariably lies on the mesenteric aspect of the adjacent alimentary tract, shares a common muscular coat and mesenteric blood supply, and is lined by gastrointestinal-type epithelium. Ectopic gastric mucosa, present in a substantial minority, secretes acid that ulcerates the lining or adjacent bowel and produces haemorrhage or perforation; ectopic pancreatic tissue may also occur. Progressive accumulation of secretions within a non-communicating cyst causes mass effect, obstruction, or a lead point for intussusception or volvulus.
additionalInvestigations: abdominal ultrasound to demonstrate the gut-signature double-wall sign
contrast-enhanced CT to define anatomy and relationship to bowel
MRI, particularly for thoracic and spinal involvement
technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy for ectopic gastric mucosa
contrast luminal studies to assess communication
spinal imaging when a thoracic duplication is identified
redFlags: gastrointestinal haemorrhage suggesting ectopic gastric mucosa
features of bowel obstruction, volvulus, or intussusception
acute abdomen from perforation or intracystic haemorrhage
respiratory compromise from a thoracic duplication
new solid or nodular components raising concern for rare malignant change in adults
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent following complete surgical excision, which is curative. Malignant transformation is rare and largely confined to lesions presenting in adulthood.
pitfalls: mistaking the cyst for another abdominal cystic lesion and overlooking its shared wall with native bowel
failing to resect adjacent bowel when the shared blood supply precludes simple enucleation, leading to incomplete removal
overlooking ectopic gastric mucosa as the source of occult bleeding
missing an associated spinal or vertebral anomaly in thoracic duplications
attempting enucleation of a long tubular duplication and leaving retained mucosa
management: Undertake complete surgical excision, which is curative, usually resecting the shared-wall bowel segment with anastomosis
Resuscitate and correct anaemia preoperatively where bleeding or obstruction has occurred
Address ectopic gastric mucosa as the source of peptic ulceration and haemorrhage, using acid suppression as a temporising measure
Treat acute complications such as obstruction, volvulus or intussusception with the cyst as lead point by urgent surgery
Obtain spinal imaging and involve neurosurgery where a thoracic duplication is associated with vertebral anomalies
Provide paediatric surgical follow-up after resection
